description: Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent, is the god of Mesoamerican civilization. His myth mixes creation, exile and a fatal meeting with Cortés.

hero.hook: God, king and prophecy: the Feathered Serpent runs through two thousand years of Mexican history.

blocks.text: **Quetzalcoatl**, the “Feathered Serpent,” is one of the richest figures of pre-Columbian Mexico. He was worshipped for more than two thousand years, from [[Teotihuacán]], the great city of the central plateau, to the Aztecs, and among the Maya under the name [[Kukulkán]].
He joins the earth (the serpent) and the sky (the feather). God of civilization, of knowledge and of moral order, he ends up meeting real history: the Spanish conquest of **1519**.
In [[Nahuatl]], **Quetzalcoatl** comes from [[quetzal]], the bird with the green feathers, and *coatl*, the serpent. That union makes him the bridge between the human and the divine.

blocks.caption: Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent: earth and sky intertwined

blocks.text: In the [[Five Suns Cosmogony]], he goes down into [[Mictlán]], the world of the dead, to bring back the bones of earlier humans. He gives them life again with his own blood. Then he steals **maize** from the ants: the founding food of Mexico. As god of the wind, he also clears the way for the rains of [[Tlaloc]].
A quetzal's tail feathers can reach **60 cm**. Among the Maya and the Aztecs, killing the bird could cost you your life: a few feathers were taken, then the bird was set free again.

The myth also has a historical face: **Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl**, priest-king of **Tula** in the 10th century. He is said to have tried to reform the cult and to replace human sacrifice with offerings of flowers and butterflies.

blocks.caption: Tula, the Toltec city tied to the reign and the fall of Quetzalcoatl

blocks.text: His rival **Tezcatlipoca** pushes him into drinking pulque, a fermented drink. Humiliated, the king goes into exile toward the east. Legend says he promises to come back in a year called “One Reed.” That promise will weigh heavily.
After he leaves, Quetzalcoatl sometimes becomes the Morning Star: the planet Venus. The god does not die, he changes form.

In **1519**, **Hernán Cortés** lands in the east, in the year “One Reed” of the Aztec calendar, the very year the god was expected back. The emperor **Moctezuma II** hesitates: should he fight an invader or welcome a god?

blocks.caption: 1519: the arrival of Cortés meets the promise of a god's return

blocks.text: He sends gifts of gold and feathers. The [[Conquistadors]] read them as an invitation. The myth, true or blown up after the fact, becomes a psychological weapon in the fall of [[Tenochtitlán]], the Aztec capital.

blocks.text: After the conquest, Quetzalcoatl does not disappear. Some friars believe they can see an apostle in him. Later, independent Mexico makes him an emblem of pre-Columbian greatness. The muralists of the 20th century, such as Diego Rivera, paint him as the soul of the country.
Even today, the Feathered Serpent still speaks of an identity: roots in the earth, ambition turned toward the sky.
**Quetzalcoatl**, the Feathered Serpent, is the god of Mesoamerican civilization. Creator, exiled king, then fatal prophecy in **1519**, he remains a central symbol of Mexico.

sections.title: A symbol that will not die
